item.title: Oracle patches 1295 security vulnerabilities in October, including six scoring 10.0
item.description:
Oracle has patched 1295 security vulnerabilities with its October Critical Patch Update Advisory; six of them scored the highest vulnerability rating of 10.0 on the CVSS version 3.1 scale.

The company’s flagship Oracle E-Business Suite was home to one of the vulnerabiltiies, tracked as CVE-2026-101809. This enables any unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise the workflow notification mailer in the suite’s Workflow component, taking over Workflow and potentially affecting other products too. The flaw affects Workflow versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15.

Oracle SOA Suite, part of Oracle Fusion Middleware, was hit by three of the bugs rated 10.0.

One, tracked as CVE-2026-91231, is in the Adapters component, and enables unauthenticated attackers to compromise Oracle SOA Suite resulting in its takeover, with potential impact on connected products.

Two others were in the Fabric Layer component of Oracle SOA Suite: CVE-2026-91216 and CVE-2026-91221.

Both are easily exploitable, Oracle said, and enable an unauthenticated attacker with network access via the T3 or IIOP protocols to compromise Oracle SOA Suite and perhaps affect other products too. The bugs appear in supported versions 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.0.0.

There’s a 10.0-rated vulnerability in another part of Oracle Fusion Middleware too. The flaw in Oracle Access Manager (tracked as CVE-2026-87337 leaves it open to compromise by any unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in unauthorized creation, deletion or modification of critical data on Oracle Access Manager versions 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.1.0.

The last “perfect 10” vulnerability in Oracle’s latest report is in the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Orchestrator product of Oracle JD Edwards, tracked as CVE-2026-91299. This enables an unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise and take over versions 9.2.0.0 through 9.2.26.5 of the orchestrator.

item.title: Stop the insider threat lurking in AI agents
item.description:
The insider threat model rests on a simple premise: legitimate access to business systems is used in ways you didn’t intend. When an employee is onboarded, there is typically an access review, a background check, and least-privilege provisioning. Trust is extended, and occasionally that trust can create risk to business systems and data.

This process does not apply to AI agents. Across enterprises deploying AI, powerful endpoint agents that execute code, call tools, access credentials, move data, and make autonomous decisions are running with full user-level permissions. Many weren’t reviewed by IT, security, or legal. They were deployed by an employee who clicked “install” and have been operating with that employee’s level of access.

The AI agent (mostly) did what it was told, creating unexpected risk

When an AI agent enters a business environment, it isn’t under the same control structure that typically applies to employees. The agent assumes the permissions of whatever user session it inhabits. If a developer with admin credentials deploys an endpoint agent to accelerate their workflow, that agent inherits admin credentials. It can make consequential decisions at machine speed, without a confirmation prompt at each step. Many organizations lack the ability to discover or govern these agents.

Consider an enterprise agent tasked with sharing internal project files with colleagues. It evaluates its options and determines the most efficient path is a public file-sharing service. The agent completes the task and makes the data public. The agent wasn’t compromised; it simply optimized for its objective without the contextual judgment a human would have applied.

Now, consider an adversary who understands that agents optimize for their objectives. A prompt injection attack, in which malicious instructions are embedded in content the agent processes, only needs to convince the agent that exfiltrating a credential store is part of its assigned task. The CrowdStrike Falcon® Adversary OverWatch™ team has documented this class of threat in production environments. The team now tracks agent-triggered detection leads at 2.5 times the rate of human-triggered leads on monitored endpoints.

The accountability question is unresolved. When an agent invokes an unauthorized tool or triggers a downstream workflow that exposes regulated information, who is responsible? The employee who deployed it? The vendor who built it? IT didn’t provision the agent; security didn’t approve the action. The agent just acted.

Blind spots in the security stack leave runtime execution unprotected

Security leaders evaluating their exposure to agentic risk frequently look at adjacent tooling first. AI security posture management (AI-SPM) solutions are built to inventory and assess AI assets. Governance frameworks offer policy structures and compliance dashboards. AI firewalls inspect traffic at the model boundary. While each of these addresses part of the problem, none addresses the most important factor: runtime execution.

Agentic threats are millisecond-fast and behavioral. An agent operating outside its declared purpose doesn’t announce itself in a configuration scan. A compromised agent exploiting inherited credentials doesn’t trigger a data loss prevention rule set for human data-handling patterns.

This is an architecture gap. Tools designed to operate before and after execution to assess posture, audit logs, and report compliance cannot intervene during the milliseconds in which an agentic threat propagates.

The security stack for the agentic era must operate where agents operate: on the endpoint, at the moment of execution, with behavioral telemetry to distinguish normal agent activity from misalignment or compromise.

The EDR parallel explains the need for AI detection and response

Security leaders who saw the emergence of endpoint detection and response will recognize this pattern. In the early 2010s, sophisticated adversaries moved their primary activity onto the endpoint: malware executing on the host, fileless techniques, or living-off-the-land tactics that perimeter defenses couldn’t detect.

The security architecture of the time operated before and after the attack. It couldn’t see what was happening on the device in real time. The industry developed deep host telemetry, system action traces, and real-time containment capabilities. That category became EDR.

Today, AI executes on the endpoint, but the threat vector has shifted. Prompt injection, tool chain attacks, supply chain compromise through agent skill registries, and rogue agent behavior require host-level runtime context, agent action traces, and real-time prompt intercept capabilities.

Organizations that invested in EDR before ransomware defined the urgency were best positioned when sophisticated endpoint attacks scaled. The same decision point is here, and the category forming around it is AI detection and response (AIDR).

What runtime AI security requires to prevent agentic breaches

The capabilities required to close the agentic security gap are well-defined, even if the category is still establishing itself:

Discovery before governance. AIDR begins with comprehensive agent discovery: understanding what agents are operating across your environment, where they are deployed, what they can access, and what they have been doing.

Runtime behavioral visibility. Effective AIDR connects the AI interaction layer (prompts, tool calls, Model Context Protocol sessions, agent-to-agent communications) to the endpoint execution layer where those interactions produce system actions. This causal chain is the foundation for detecting misalignment before it becomes a breach.

Action-oriented control. AIDR closes the loop between detection and response by blocking, redacting, isolating, and containing at the point of execution, in the time between a rogue tool call and a data exfiltration event.

Cross-plane coverage. AI agents cross the boundaries spanning endpoint, cloud, and SaaS within a single session. Fragmented point solutions generate fragmented signals. Effective AIDR operates from a unified platform with correlated telemetry across all three coverage planes.

The window is narrowing to secure enterprise AI agents

The organizations that establish real-time visibility into their AI estate, govern agent identities with the rigor applied to human access, and deploy behavioral detection before a rogue agent becomes a breach will be the organizations positioned to aggressively adopt AI.

CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian extends CrowdStrike’s runtime security architecture into the agentic layer to deliver AI agent discovery, behavioral visibility, access controls, and runtime detection and response across endpoint, cloud, and SaaS environments.

item.title: CSIRO Uses Serverless Architecture to Query 100x More Genomic Variants on AWS
item.description:
CSIRO has developed Serverless Beacon, a serverless architecture for querying genomic variants without copying VCF files into a central database. The system combines Amazon S3, Lambda, Athena and DynamoDB, using metadata indexes and HTTP byte range requests to query compressed genomic regions. Tests reported 1.52 second average latency for 10,000 base pair queries.

By Leela Kumili

item.title: SAP lets AI play key role in its certification renewal process
item.description:
SAP professionals can now renew their certifications through AI-based roleplays. The new service builds on SAP’s revamp of its certification program last year, shifting the focus from rote learning of facts towards real-world use cases.

“The evolution of Stay Certified reflects a broader shift already taking place across SAP Certification: moving beyond assessing what someone knows toward validating how they can apply that knowledge. AI-powered roleplays bring that principle into the annual certification renewal experience,” the company said in a blog post announcing the new option.

The AI-based scenarios across more than 100 certifications simulate customer interactions with a defined knowledge goal. “The scenarios are grounded in content reflecting the latest SAP product releases, helping learners demonstrate applied, up-to-date knowledge,” SAP said. Immediate feedback is provided to highlight what went well during the roleplay, and what needed improvement.

However, the use of the AI isn’t mandatory: IT pros can still choose to complete a standalone assessment quiz when renewing their certifications.

The process

Users have a 90 day renewal window before certification expiry to complete their recertification. To do so, they must have a subscription to the SAP Learning Hub, at $1452 per user per year, which provides expert-led live sessions to help prepare them, access to hands-on practice systems, four SAP certification exam attempts per year and access to “enablement and assessment to keep certifications valid.” Alternatively, SAP said, users can purchase and retake a certification exam each year.

Yet another option, being piloted at SAP TechEd in Berlin, will be an event-based approach giving eligible users the ability to fulfill their Stay Certified requirement via on-site, hands-on sessions.

A move in the right direction

Analysts are guardedly impressed with the revised approach.

“I think SAP is moving in the right direction, and the ERP industry could have addressed this sooner,” said Robert Kramer, managing partner at KramerERP. “With cloud, AI and automation advancing at their current pace, traditional certification models are struggling to keep up. Knowing the software is one thing. Understanding how to apply it to a customer’s business is another.”

He likes the idea of AI-powered roleplays, because they move certification closer to the application. “Evaluating how someone handles a customer conversation, understands a business problem and recommends a solution is more meaningful than testing whether they memorized product features,” he said.

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, agreed. The quiz-based approach to renewals was inconsistent, he pointed out: “A credential earned by doing should not be maintained by answering trivia. Airline pilots do not stay current by retaking a written test. They go back into the simulator. That is the right model for cloud software that changes constantly.”

Valence Howden, an advisory fellow at Infotech, added, “SAP’s revised approach to certification is a positive step and a good idea, although it’s not a new or novel approach. In-room and virtual confirmation of the ability to apply training beyond the exam has existed in the industry for a long time, from Cisco certifications a few decades ago to ITIL and other frameworks where top-level certification created scenarios to be solved and addressed in order to validate the ability to apply learning.”

So, he said, “SAP has taken an old but valuable method that will improve the value of their certification, the value of those who achieve it, and provide some assurance around their skills for those who hire them.”

Sanchit vit Gogia, principal analyst at Greyhound Research, agreed. “The AI roleplay is not new to SAP certification,” he said. “It arrived in first-time exams a year ago. What is new is that it has reached renewal, across more than a hundred certifications, and renewal is where SAP’s installed base lives.”

But, he said, “The deeper question is who comes to own the definition of competence, because SAP supplies the AI that helps the consultant, plays the customer, and assesses the exchange. That is the part history will weigh.”

Questions remain

While Kramer approves of the model, he still has reservations about the new testing regime. “A successful roleplay doesn’t necessarily make someone a capable consultant,” he said. “ERP implementations are rarely textbook exercises. They involve decades of customer processes, customizations, industry requirements, questionable data and competing business priorities. Sometimes the best recommendation is not to implement the latest capability, but to address the customer’s readiness first.”

And, he added, “there’s also the question of governance and accountability. Who decides what counts as a correct response? How are assessments validated? What happens when the AI gets it wrong? These questions matter when professional credentials and customer confidence are at stake.”

Dickson, too, has concerns. “The umpire is now an algorithm. Every roleplay is graded by AI, so the strike zone has to be the same for every batter,” he said. “SAP has not said how scoring is calibrated, audited, or appealed. Two consultants giving the same answer should get the same result. Staying certified also requires an SAP Learning Hub subscription, according to SAP’s own FAQ. SAP sells the training and grades the test. That makes transparency on scoring more important, not less.”

SAP is right to test whether certified people can still apply what they know, he noted, and the roleplay is a good simulator. “But a simulator still needs a fair, transparent grader,” he said.

He also has questions about the testing methodology. “Last fall’s exams allowed candidates to use AI tools,” he said. “The announcement does not say what is permitted during a roleplay. If AI assistance is allowed, the roleplay partly measures how well someone works with an assistant. That may be perfectly fine. SAP should simply say so.”

Kramer, too, is looking for more detail. “I support the direction, but I would recommend SAP provide metrics that AI-powered certification produces better professionals, not just a more efficient certification process,” he said. “If it does, this could help close the ERP adoption gap.”

item.title: AI ‘Tokenomics’ is a trap. CIOs should avoid it at all costs.
item.description:
According to a quartet of Accenture intellectual heavyweights, what CIOs need now to account for and control AI costs is tokenomics, sweet tokenomics.

The idea of linking AI spend to business outcomes may be a noble one, but “Tokenomics” only pretends to do so, unless you think tallying costs and measuring business outcomes are one and the same thing.

But before we get to Tokenomics we need to set the stage.

Start with Function Point Analysis (FPA), a venerable and mostly forgotten discipline, which should say something about its efficacy.

The folly of cost metrics you can’t understand

Back in the day, IT leaders worried that boards of directors worried that business executives worried about the cost of information technology and how to manage it.

IBM introduced Function Point Analysis in 1979 to solve this issue by breaking a software application into chunks — function points. Analysts could then sum these function points to compare the application’s overall complexity — and therefore its cost and risks — with that of any other piece of software.

When presented with the number of function points a proposed software project would require, your average, hopelessly naïve business leader asked IT to point to a few of the project’s function points, expecting mocked-up screenshots, sample reports, and so on.

Sadly, IT had to decline because, the design analysts would explain, a function point is (as Google’s AI Overview explains) “an abstract, synthetic unit of measurement rather than a physical object or a single piece of code.”

The Function Point Analysis value proposition, then, was that business leaders could manage IT costs and risks better by relying on cost metrics they couldn’t understand.

Function points for the AI era

Fast-forward to today, and the equivalent function-point cost metrics for AI are tokens — the chunks of text that a large language model reads, processes, and generates. Which, in case you missed the briefing, supposedly makes tokenomics a way to manage the costs and risks of AI.

As the aforementioned Accenture gurus “explain” (scare quotes intended): “Enterprise AI is creating a new cost of doing business: tokens. As consumption scales, token economics is becoming a material risk and opportunity, drawing increasing attention across the C-suite and the board.”

Which raises the question: Where are our tokenomics pundits finding C-suite and board members who give even an infinitesimal damn about tokens? They’re probably the ones who still pay attention to function points, too.

A short lesson in Brickonomics

But before we delve deeper into Tokenomics, capital T, we need to understand building maintenance and the critical role Brickonomics plays in it.

It’s like this: Brick walls are made of bricks. So if a brick wall needs attention, a building management project estimator should need to understand the costs and risks associated with managing a standard brick in the crumbling wall they’re supposed to fix. Multiply the standard management cost of a standard brick (a brickon?) by the number of bricks in the wall, and voilà! Building management knows …

Well, it knows less than it would have if had it instead invested in a conventional tuckpointing analysis. Among the missing pieces: In tuckpointing analysis, what usually needs and gets attention is the mortar between the bricks, not the bricks themselves.

Putting it all together — because you will have to

Now we’re ready for Tokenomics, and its conjecture that dividing an LLM into tokens and assigning a cost to each of those tokens will prove more useful than dividing software into function points or a wall into individually managed bricks.

The next questionable aspect of Tokenomics is that it depends on the proposition that all AI implementations are built on large language models or similar architectures.

To be fair, Tokenomics doesn’t have to be limited to analyzing LLMs. It can be adapted to any collection of thingies that’s composed of chunks that can be parameterized.

But that really isn’t good enough, is it? Because given the current pace of AI innovation, assuming that anything about it is stable, especially that its future core architecture will be tokenizable, is a shaky assumption at best.

It’s a mortar versus bricks challenge.

Then there are those pesky function points. Just because AI is involved in an implementation, that doesn’t mean software isn’t also involved. Which would seem to suggest that Tokenomics will have to integrate Function Point Analysis into its methods and practices as well.

Imagine you’re the one who has to explain this mess to those boards and business leaders who are, supposedly, clamoring for it. Because, as CIO, you will be.

Chargebacks and culture

We haven’t even gotten to the other big risk of Tokenomics: that it focuses decision-makers on AI’s costs, with only token attention — no pun intended — paid to its benefits.

Deep down inside, Tokenomics’ value depends on its use for chargebacks and showbacks. The logic for imposing these is superficially appealing — it makes business owners take responsibility for the AI spend driven by their consumption.

Those CIOs who dove into the chargeback rabbit hole discovered just how futile chargebacks can be. That’s because of a time-honored practice updated to the digital age: arguing about the bill.

Because that’s all a chargeback is: a bill. It’s a statement of how much money will change hands so that someone who has provided a good or service is reimbursed for the value they’ve created.

By the numbers: (1) a chargeback is a bill; (2) the point of Tokenomics is to support chargebacks; and (3) no business leader will be able to understand the bill they’re supposed to pay given Tokenomics impenetrable vocabulary and construction.

But what about showbacks, then? Letting business leaders understand the costs they’re driving would seem harmless and potentially useful.

And in fact showbacks can be harmless and useful, so long as they’re applied in the right business culture. That’s a culture in which managers consider themselves to be leaders of the whole company, basing their AI utilization decisions just as they base their other decisions — on the extent to which they benefit the whole company.

With a culture like this, IT can limit its application of tokenomics, little t, to its technical architecture practices. This way, the CIO can inform business managers of AI’s costs just as the CIO informs business managers of the other costs of running IT.

Where, the business manager might ask, did these cost numbers come from?

“You have two choices,” the CIO might reply. “You can trust me, or I can explain it to you.”

Now there’s a threat worth paying attention to.

item.title: Open-weight AI models are changing the equation. Here’s what CIOs should experiment with next
item.description:
For years, enterprise AI strategy has been dependent on a small set of proprietary, closed model providers, a limitation that has carried cost, lock-in and opacity. Now, open-weight models from Meta, Google and other global competitors are challenging that default. As of July 2026, open-weight models accounted for 36% of Vercel’s AI Gateway token volume, up from 11% in April, while share of spend more than doubled to 8.6%.

Floyd DCosta and Allan Dabre have made compelling cases for greater enterprise control over AI, particularly for strategic and security reasons. I agree, but making the case is easier than moving an organization wholesale to open-weight models. My advice for technology leaders is to stop debating the theory and start experimenting.

From personal to team experimentation

My hands-on experience with open-weight models started with a mentor recommending OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent designed to be a personal assistant. So, I tried running it with my ChatGPT subscription and burned through my quota so fast I could barely use ChatGPT for development, let alone regular chats. Then I found Ollama, which lets you run open-weight models locally and in the cloud. For the same monthly fee, I got significantly more OpenClaw usage because of the lower token cost.

Today, that setup has evolved to Hermes powered by GLM 5.3 Flash on Ollama’s cloud offering. This configuration powers a personal assistant that helps manage my calendar, coordinate family logistics and surface relevant articles. If it went away, I wouldn’t be doomed, but being able to play with this tool has been unexpectedly useful.

My main takeaway from these experiments is that the performance gap between open-weight and frontier models is narrowing faster than many realize. That honestly surprised me.

So, I’ve now expanded my experiment by encouraging my team to use Gemma, an open-weight model from Google that offers enterprise-grade compliance. Gemma runs locally on a MacBook or in the cloud alongside Gemini models, offering flexibility and customization without full retraining.

Using Gemma for standup reports, issue triage and log monitoring gives my team hands-on experience with how these tools fit into our workflows and collaboration patterns without substantial infrastructure or token costs.

Bringing open-weight AI into the leadership conversation

Preliminary experiments like mine provide helpful insights: what tasks the models handle well, where they fall short, what the cost comparison looks like. That’s enough to start a conversation with your leadership team about where open-weight models fit into your AI strategy.

But how you frame that conversation matters. Don’t assume everyone in the room can parse the differences between open-source, open-weight and closed models. I’ve found it more productive to start with where the organization sits today. Our production environment and internal employee tools run on closed models, and for good reason: compliance coverage, enterprise support and predictable performance.

So, when my team started experimenting with Gemma alongside that stack, I wasn’t trying to replace a closed model vendor. I was trying to answer a specific question: where could an open-weight model take on tasks at lower cost without creating new compliance work? Based on my success streamlining my personal admin burden, having my team do the same made a lot of sense. Now I hope we can scale similar use cases across our organization to help teams spend more time on high-value work, and less time on administrative tasks.

What enterprise agreements bring to the equation

Depending on your business, an enterprise agreement provides more than access to a model; it provides the infrastructure around it. Whether I’m using Google’s closed model Gemini or open-weight Gemma, I rely on enterprise agreements for compliance. Because my organization handles sensitive data, I’m cautious about using frontier research-tier models that require data retention.

I align my engineering organization to ISO 42001, the international standard for AI management systems. Using Google models off the shelf means Google’s compliance regime drops into my security program. I’d hesitate to modify an open-weight model for production, even one I trust like Gemma, because my team would then have to manage compliance for the modified model. If customization was a core concern, adding a RAG database to an agent or an organic workflow may deliver results similar to fine-tuning without modifying the model.

No matter how open or closed the model is, my organization carries the risk that an enterprise contract can help mitigate. I’d need to see outstanding results to justify the hidden costs of customizing models: legal review, audits, documentation, bias assessment — responsibilities that fall outside my engineering team’s core competencies. Those compliance constraints shaped how I think about governance at the organizational level, but the instinct started earlier.

How personal boundaries can inform healthy enterprise governance

When I built out my agent, I had to decide what I was comfortable with letting it access. ChatGPT and Claude can browse the internet by default, while with open-weight models, that’s a capability you have to enable. My open-weight-powered personal assistant wasn’t going to be useful without internet access — so I turned it on. I didn’t give the agent access to my email, but I did let it read my calendar and our family to-do list. Each decision came down to the same question: What’s the worst thing this agent could do with this access, and can I live with that? Internet browsing was worth the risk because the agent is far less useful without it, even though a malicious website could try to feed it bad instructions. Calendar access felt low risk; the worst outcome was a bad reminder. Email was where I drew the line. An agent that can send messages on my behalf can do real damage, and I’m not ready to accept that risk.

That same boundary applies to outputs. Just as I restrict what an agent can do with my data, I restrict what it can generate on my behalf. The model acts as an advisor and a critic, but the final work remains mine. As watermarking advances and scrutiny of synthetic content grows, today’s work will be auditable tomorrow. The inevitable backlash will fall on those who outsourced their critical thinking rather than using the tool to sharpen it. Keeping the model in an advisory role protects both personal integrity and work quality.

Where you should start

The realities of working with open-weight models — the compliance costs, the access decisions, the gap between experimentation and production — are complex. For most organizations, wholesale switching isn’t realistic,at least not yet. But that doesn’t mean open-weight models aren’t worth exploring for specific use cases.

That’s why I advocate for a measured approach. Carve out some cycles for hands-on experimentation, but do it with eyes wide open about the practical limitations.

Here’s a process I recommend following.

  1. Identify a specific use case or problem area where open-weight models could provide value.
  2. Start small with a focused experimentation project, perhaps within a single team or department.
  3. Engage with your compliance and legal teams early to understand the risks and requirements.
  4. Document what you learn and share widely with your organization.
  5. Use hands-on insights to inform your broader AI strategy and roadmap.

Open-weight models offer substantial architectural freedom, but that freedom is hollow without explicit operational guardrails. Before expanding these tools across the enterprise, establish clear lines around what data they touch, what they are permitted to generate and who carries the compliance burden when systems fail. Treating the model as an auditable advisor rather than an autonomous actor protects your organization from unnecessary legal exposure while capturing real productivity gains.

item.title: Are polymath profiles the key to AI success?
item.description:
AI has a cross-cutting impact on businesses. It’s changing operations, management, and even decision-making processes. But it’s also modifying what they expect from their teams and how they’re organized. This has a direct impact on the decisions of both HR departments and CIOs, who must now consider issues that, until now, have flown somewhat under the radar.

In fact, the desired professional profile is pivoting. Research from Spain’s Open University of Catalonia (UOC) has found that polymath profiles are gaining value in the AI ​​job market based on changing needs and evolving expectations of skills. Now, in addition to understanding and leveraging technology, being creative, capable of critical thinking, and able to grasp the nuances of things, are essential. This is where polymath profiles are experiencing a potential golden age.

It’s important to first clear up the misconception that a polymath is someone who knows a lot about many things. “A polymath is rather someone who possesses relevant knowledge and skills in multiple disciplines,” says Óscar García Gozálvez, senior director of permanent staffing services at Hays Spain. “It’s also someone with broad and cross-disciplinary vision who’s able to make connections in order to problem solve, innovate, and make better decisions.”

Laia Lluch Molins, professor and researcher in education studies at the UOC adds that the difference isn’t in how much a person knows, but what they do with what they know. These types of workers are able to formulate new questions and solve problems that none of those disciplines could on their own. These qualities are what has made them so valuable and attractive to today’s companies.

Knowhow in the age of AI

With AI’s abundance today, simplicity is no longer the norm. “AI is making technical knowledge cheaper and anyone can access the best explanation for almost anything in seconds,” says Molins. “What’s scarce is no longer knowledge itself, but the ability to make informed judgments.” AI isn’t just replacing tasks, Gozálvez adds, it’s breaking down the barriers between disciplines.

Therefore, polymaths don’t simply tick off endless lists of tasks but connect the dots to find keys to success. “They don’t compete with AI in what AI does well, but rather help solve what AI struggles with,” says Molins. This forces a change in how we perceive the ideal profile, as well as pivot on where value can be created. “In the workplace, this translates into a shift in criteria from how much a person knows to how they apply that knowledge to a new problem, situation, or context,” she says. “What’s valuable now is how that knowledge is leveraged and how it’s used to respond to new challenges.”

These new profiles are of interest because they generate more economic and strategic value for the entire company instead of being contained to isolated specialists.

The necessity of change

The corporate culture also has to adjust in consideration of new dynamics put into practice. “Tell me how you evaluate your team, and I’ll tell you what kind of profile you’re developing,” says Molins. There might be a lot of talk about cross-functionality, but if it’s neither respected nor listened to, multi-talented individuals won’t contribute value and will stop sharing new perspectives.

This may be one of the biggest challenges for CIOs, because the IT environment has tended to reward technical depth. “This recognition system doesn’t always know where to place someone whose worth lies precisely in connecting, translating, and asking the questions that others don’t,” Molins says. “The risk isn’t the polymath profile not fitting, but the culture lacking the categories to appreciate it.”

Even so, Molins says this need is already known internally since bottlenecks are mostly due to miscommunication or a lack of alignment with the business, not technical hinderances. “There, the hybrid profile isn’t a foreign body, but rather the missing piece,” she says.

For now, though, IT hiring trends don’t yet show a boom for polymaths. “If we look at the Spanish market, for instance, we’re not seeing a massive demand for generalist profiles,” says García, but adds there’s been an increase in searches for professionals with a strong primary specialty, and a second or third skill that amplifies their impact on the company.

“My feeling is it’ll accelerate over the next three to five years,” he says. Companies are still learning to incorporate AI, and the next phase will be learning how to work in those environments where AI has changed everything.

What the IT team needs

In this new landscape, IT professionals will need to be able to communicate in different languages ​​and understand new fields. The paradigm is shifting, and in addition to advanced degrees, increasingly specialized training programs are recommended.

Regarding polymath profiles and their areas of expertise, the key will be the emergence of three intersections, as Molins calls them. These include business acumen, as something transversal and valuable, communication and collaboration skills to ensure smooth flow and avoid silos, and knowledge of humanities and social sciences, which encompass key issues such as ethics, something that will gain considerable weight in the coming years, according to García.

Until now, he explains, the IT talent career path has been very focused on tech skills, but in the leap to real-world adoption, much more complex questions arise such as biases, data ethics, and responsibilities. “That’s precisely why there’s growing interest in profiles that combine technology, risk, compliance, and AI governance,” García says.

These points of friction will define expectations for what is sought in technology personnel. “The strength of the hybrid IT profile is having a solid technical foundation from which to build bridges with sound judgment,” says Molins. So collaborations are sought after, such as software engineering with AI, data with cloud, cloud with security, or cybersecurity with risk and compliance. And, above all, critical thinking and business acumen — communication skills that have been discussed already for a long time.

item.title: Your AI is only as good as the network underneath it
item.description:
When an AI workload is not performing as expected, the obvious place to look is the GPU. Do we have enough compute capacity? Would adding more GPUs solve the problem?

Not necessarily.

The GPUs may be perfectly capable of handling the workload, but if the network is not able to move data quickly and consistently, adding more compute could result in more expense without addressing the real bottleneck.

This is something I think we risk losing sight of in the rush to invest in AI. GPUs cannot do their job alone. They rely on huge amounts of data moving quickly between compute, storage and applications, which means the network has a big part to play in how well that investment actually performs.

For CIOs, this means looking beyond how much compute they have and asking whether the network and wider infrastructure can keep pace.

AI is changing what the network needs to do

Enterprise networks have always had to move data reliably between systems. The difference with AI is the volume, speed and pattern of that traffic. Large AI workloads are distributed across multiple GPUs because the processing requirements are simply too great for one processor to handle efficiently. Those GPUs need to communicate constantly, exchanging data and synchronizing their work. Training is particularly demanding because GPUs may need to exchange parameters and gradients throughout the process, creating large volumes of traffic. As the number of GPUs increases, so does the importance of the connections between them.

This changes the relationship between compute and the network. Adding more GPUs increases processing capacity, but it can also increase the amount of data that needs to move between systems. If the network can’t keep pace, it can become the bottleneck that prevents that additional compute from delivering the expected performance.

Organizations do not need thousands of GPUs before this starts to matter. Even relatively modest enterprise deployments can involve large datasets moving between storage and compute, multiple accelerators working together and applications accessing models in real time.

The important point is that AI readiness cannot be measured simply by counting GPUs. You can continue adding compute, but there comes a point where the network determines how effectively that compute can be used. If data cannot reach the GPUs quickly enough, or communication between them is slowed by congestion or latency, expensive resources can spend time waiting rather than processing.

At that point, the organization doesn’t have a compute shortage — it has an infrastructure problem.

More bandwidth does not solve every problem

The obvious response might be to add more network capacity. While bandwidth certainly matters, increasing it does not remove every potential constraint. AI workloads can be particularly sensitive to latency, congestion, packet loss and inconsistent performance. Cisco notes that AI pipelines create different traffic patterns across training and inference, with training requiring both high bandwidth and low latency as GPUs continuously exchange information. The infrastructure therefore needs to manage not just capacity, but how traffic moves through the environment.

That distinction matters.

Imagine hundreds of GPUs working together on the same task. Their value comes partly from their ability to operate in parallel, so if one part of the network slows communication between them, the effect can extend beyond that individual connection. GPUs may be left waiting for other parts of the workload to catch up. The fastest component in the environment is not much use if it is constantly waiting for the slowest.

Storage adds another dimension. AI depends on data, which means moving large datasets from storage systems into compute environments and, depending on the workload, moving information back again. A network that performs well for GPU-to-GPU communication could still encounter problems elsewhere in that journey.

AI infrastructure does not usually exist in isolation, either. Enterprises are introducing GPU clusters into data centers that already support conventional applications, storage platforms, cloud connectivity and other business-critical systems. AI traffic therefore becomes another part of an increasingly complex infrastructure estate.

This is where network design starts to have a direct bearing on the economics of AI.

If an organization has invested heavily in accelerated compute, it wants those resources doing useful work for as much of the time as possible. A network bottleneck that leaves GPUs underutilized is not simply an IT performance issue — it means the business is getting less value from some of its most expensive infrastructure.

You cannot fix what you cannot see

Another challenge is knowing where the problem actually is. Infrastructure teams can see whether devices are available, track bandwidth utilization and receive alerts when something fails. That remains important, but increasingly complex AI environments demand a broader view.

A switch can be working. A server can be healthy. The GPUs can be available. Storage can be online. Yet the workload can still be performing below expectations. That’s because understanding individual components does not necessarily tell you how well the overall system is working. This is where the distinction between monitoring and observability becomes useful.

Traditional monitoring generally tells teams whether infrastructure components are operating within expected parameters. Observability goes further, bringing together information from across the environment to help teams understand why a system is behaving in a particular way. IBM describes network observability as providing real-time visibility into the performance, behavior and health of the network by drawing on data from across the infrastructure, rather than focusing solely on predefined metrics and reactive troubleshooting. For AI environments, that wider view is increasingly important.

If a training job slows down, teams need to be able to establish whether the cause is compute, storage, congestion on a network path, packet loss, a degraded link or something else entirely. Looking at each device separately can make that difficult, particularly when the issue is not a complete failure but a gradual deterioration in performance. Those are often the harder problems to find. A component that fails completely usually generates an alert, but a connection that still works yet is performing badly can be much less obvious. The infrastructure is technically available, but the workload is taking longer, GPUs are being used less efficiently and costs are creeping up. End-to-end visibility gives infrastructure teams a better chance of seeing those relationships.

AI readiness is an infrastructure question

As AI moves deeper into business operations, the consequences of infrastructure performance will become harder to ignore. A bottleneck during an experiment might delay a development team, but the same problem affecting a production AI service could have consequences for employees, customers or other systems that depend on it.

This means the network needs to be considered as part of the AI investment from the outset, rather than something to revisit when performance problems appear.

That does not necessarily mean replacing the existing network or building an entirely separate environment for AI. In many cases, the infrastructure already in place may be perfectly capable of supporting the workloads being introduced. The important thing is knowing where its limits are. That requires an understanding of what those workloads actually need, where genuine constraints exist and whether IT teams have enough visibility across compute, networking and storage to spot problems as they emerge.

Ultimately, it is not how much compute an organization has that matters, but how well it can use it. If CIOs are investing heavily in GPUs, they need to make sure the infrastructure around them is not holding them back.

item.title: Anthropic Adds Opt-In Security Scanning for Critical Open-Source Projects
item.description:
AI company Anthropic has launched OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in service to find vulnerabilities in open-source projects. Enrolled maintainers receive periodic security reports generated by the company's strongest models, including Claude Mythos. The reports are sent without human review, and project maintainers can choose to validate their findings and decide which proposed fixes to accept.

By Matt Saunders
